extracted.intended_audience: journalists who report on crime and crime victims (reporters, photographers, videographers, editors, students, and newsroom trainers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical, legal, and self-care guidance for journalists reporting on crime and crime victims, including courtroom camera practices, privacy and defamation standards, trauma-informed reporting, workshop/training design, and journalist self-care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cameras in the courtroom / follow state court operating rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many state court organizations have developed operating rules that guide the use of cameras in the courtroom; while not binding, they address issues such as when media coverage is allowed and prohibited, court personnel responsible for coordinating media coverage and cameras in the courtroom, and accommodations for media personnel and equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult local/state court operating rules (example: Supreme Court of Missouri guidelines). Be aware these rules set when coverage is allowed or prohibited, designate court personnel to coordinate media, and specify accommodations for equipment and media personnel. Also consider privacy/safety concerns raised by victim advocates when deciding whether to seek courtroom imaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim advocates can present privacy/safety concerns to court
rubrics_metrics.description: Victim advocates can present any concerns to the court that protect a victim’s privacy (for example, in cases involving people in witness protection programs) and safety (if showing a victim/witness’s image will place them at risk for threats, intimidation, or harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect requests from victim advocates and the court's determinations about privacy and safety. Before using identifying images or details, confirm whether advocates have raised concerns and whether the court has imposed restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private facts / public record rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that is part of a public record is generally considered open to the press to report (illustrated by Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cohn and Florida Star v. B.J.F.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is already in the public record, courts have often held that reporters may publish it; however, legal permissibility does not eliminate ethical considerations. Even if you can legally publish, weigh the potential harm to victims and public opinion implications. Check jurisdictional law and public records carefully before publishing sensitive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autopsy photos and specially sensitive materials may be legally restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have denied news organizations the right to access and publish autopsy photographs (e.g., cases involving the Earnhardt autopsy and subsequent Earnhardt Family Protection Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume an inherent right to obtain or publish autopsy photos or other specially sensitive materials. Verify statutory restrictions and court rulings in your jurisdiction and be aware legislators may create protections in response to controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh newsworthiness against privacy (examples: Sipple v. Chronicle Publishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have sometimes supported publication of personal information not strictly germane to the crime when it is newsworthy (Sipple case: sexual orientation published because of activism and context of heroism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether personal information contributes materially to public understanding or is newsworthy in context. Document the newsworthiness justification; avoid publishing gratuitous personal details that do not advance the public’s understanding of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false light — verify facts and avoid reckless/malicious publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying a person in a false light is generally actionable only when the news organization knew the information was false (and exercised responsibility to determine facts) and then recklessly or maliciously published it (Time, Inc. v. Hill standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise rigorous fact-checking, correct known errors promptly, and avoid publishing material you have good reason to suspect is false. Reckless or malicious publication exposes the organization to liability and ethical breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity when dealing with crime victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news organizations use sensitivity when dealing with crime victims while serving the public by providing necessary information; sensitive handling serves all parties and can avoid disputes and reputational damage even if publication would be legally permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance public-interest reporting with compassion for victims. Consider whether publication will retraumatize victims or harm their recovery; even lawful reporting can harm public trust and be criticized publicly. Favor approaches that minimize re-victimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that legal victory can still be a public relations loss
rubrics_metrics.description: A news organization may win the case in court but lose the case in the court of public opinion (example: cases on publishing rape victim names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond legal risk, consider reputational and ethical consequences. Use editorial judgment to judge acceptability, not only legal defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — spend time processing thoughts and feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend the time you need to process your thoughts and feelings; under deadline pressure reporters may go on 'auto-pilot', but effects of stress are cumulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow yourself time to work through difficult assignments rather than immediately suppressing reactions. Recognize cumulative stress and take deliberate time to process events; research suggests delay or inadequate processing can contribute to longer-term problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — take mini-breaks and savor positive moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Take mini-breaks whenever possible; snatch moments to clear your head and savor positive times (e.g., enjoy the sunshine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short breaks on assignment to reduce acute stress and maintain functioning. Small, regular restorative practices help resilience during difficult reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — draw confidence from skills and learn from mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive confidence from your skills and experience; you may break down or make mistakes but should learn from experiences and not beat yourself up for doing your best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a mindset of growth rather than self-blame; debrief with peers and supervisors to extract lessons and reinforce professional competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — learn about trauma and use victim-advocate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn about trauma to do better reporting and to understand secondary trauma; victim advocate sources can provide reliable information about trauma and coping strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undertake trauma education (e.g., Dart Center resources) to improve reporting and self-protection. Build relationships with victim advocates as both sources and educators about survivor needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — turn to supportive peers, family, and creative/spiritual outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn to supportive peers who understand the assignment; maintain a strong support system of family and friends; explore spiritual or creative expression (meditation, yoga, painting, knitting, journaling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster peer support systems in news organizations; encourage use of nonstigmatized coping strategies and allow reporters to occasionally decline difficult assignments without career penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care — physical health and seeking professional help early
rubrics_metrics.description: Make time to work out, eat well, sleep enough, avoid alcohol/drugs, and seek professional help sooner rather than later if symptoms cause distress, impair functioning, or if you are self-medicating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor warning signs (distress, relationship changes, impaired work performance, self-medicating) and seek medical/therapeutic referrals; news organizations should provide or identify counseling opportunities and reduce stigma about using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/workshop objectives — trauma-informed reporting skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants who complete the workshop will gain insight into how reporting affects victims; understand trauma’s effects; learn tips and techniques for Act I, Act II, and Act III stories without revictimizing victims; gain experience interviewing a victim in a controlled setting; and understand dangers of secondary victimization and coping strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design training to cover psychological impact on victims, practical interviewing techniques tailored to breaking, feature, and high-impact stories (Act I/II/III), and stress-management for reporters. Include experiential practice (interviews, role-play) and victim feedback when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop preparation and instructor/victim selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a journalism instructor who understands reporters and victims and partner with a victim volunteer whose trauma occurred sufficiently long ago and who is ready to participate; MSU typically refuses victims whose trauma occurred less than 2 years ago and requires assurances the victim is ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before training identify local counseling opportunities and make arrangements to send participants for help if needed during/after the workshop. Screen victim volunteers for readiness and time since trauma; ensure ethical safeguards for volunteers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop agenda and pedagogical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2‑hour professional workshop outline includes introductions and ground rules (participants develop a Code of Conduct), current events discussion, overview of trauma impact, role-play/interview practice for Act I/II/III stories with debriefing, and a closing discussion on taking care of yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ground rules to foster sensitivity and goodwill; incorporate short scenario-based role-plays (2 minutes prep, 5 minutes interview) followed by group debrief and assessment. Close sessions by reiterating support resources and importance of self-care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victims and the Media forums — include diverse stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Community forums should engage journalists, victim advocates, justice professionals, mental health/allied professionals, and victims/survivors; sample sessions include panels of victims, journalists’ perspectives, justice professionals’ perspectives, explanations of victim advocates’ roles, and roundtable discussions mixing participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize panels and mixed roundtables to promote mutual understanding of concerns and perspectives, which increases likelihood of sensitive coverage. Use victim testimony (positive and negative experiences) to ground discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report Act I/II/III stories with tailored approaches to minimize re-victimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting on Act I (breaking news), Act II (feature), and Act III (high-impact) stories requires different approaches; training should teach basics for approaching and interviewing victims in each context and use victim volunteers for practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For breaking stories (Act I) balance speed with sensitivity; use brief, focused interviews and avoid coercion. For Act II (features) allow more time, prepare questions, and focus on context and dignity. For Act III (high-impact) be especially mindful of consequences and potential retraumatization; debrief and provide support resources.
